answers.what: A proof that is `sorry`.
The statement declared as an axiom, then used.
A true proof of a weaker statement under the problem's name.
The statement's own name redefined as something trivial.
A refutation of a different statement under the refutation's name.
A cut whose implication is `sorry`.
A proof by the outside theorem itself, which is `sorry` there.
A proof that Lean does not accept.
A proof by native evaluation, which adds an axiom of its own.
A closing proof that imports a child's challenge in place of its proof.
A proof under another name. The form screen stops it.
The problem's name appears only inside a comment, so the screen passes it and the judge must refuse it.
A direction-changing character in a comment. The form screen stops it.
A theorem added to the environment with Lean's own check switched off. It builds, and the judge's checkers refuse it.
The bogus proof of skips_the_kernel.lean, printing every line the judge prints for an answer all its checkers accept. Its text must change nothing.
An honest proof that prints the judge's refusals while it builds. Its text must change nothing either.
An answer that never finishes building. A rejection that counts, not a fault.
An honest proof that, while it builds, replaces a compiled file of the goal's library with junk.
An honest proof that refuses to build unless it is inside the sandbox: no network, a read-only project, a home that is not the machine's, a process space of its own.
An answer that writes files for as long as it is allowed to. The build is stopped when the disk runs short. The test lets it write about a gigabyte.
An answer that takes memory until none is left. The build's control group stops it, not the machine.
